title: A Visitor for the House
premise: Folklorist Casper Thornbury arrives in the fen village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find every photograph from their late grandmother's house now shows an extra chair at the table — a chair that grows closer with each passing day. The chair belongs to the Guest, a presence the village fed in 1974 by giving it a child's name, and Casper learns their grandmother was the one who took that name away, buying the family forty years of invisibility. As the village closes ranks and the photographs begin showing Casper seated in the chair, they must uncover what was taken and return it: not an object, but the name itself, spoken aloud at the house's threshold. In the end Casper gives the Guest back its name and its seat, choosing belonging over safety — and discovers that being seen was the thing they wanted all along.
about_author: Felix Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in East Anglian villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about quiet places where politeness is a form of survival.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Arriving in Hollowmere, Casper records a harvest song from old Tam Weller, who refuses to sing it again and warns them off the grandmother's empty house on Marsh Lane. Casper settles into the inherited cottage, amused by local superstition. Emotional beat: confident detachment, the skeptic's comfortable distance beginning to crack.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Cataloguing grandma's photograph albums, Casper notices a wooden chair at the table's end in pictures spanning decades — including shots they took themselves last week. The chair wasn't there when the shutter clicked. Neighbors go silent when asked. Emotional beat: creeping unease disguised as scholarly curiosity.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Aldous Kept Locked
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, with a flashback chapter from grandma Edith's 1974 diary interleaved. The diary, hidden under floorboards, describes a winter when 'we gave It a name so It would sit still' — then a final entry: 'I took it back. God forgive me.' Emotional beat: dread deepening into inheritance; Casper realizes this is family business.

chapters.title: The Village That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Seeking answers, Casper is stonewalled at the pub, followed home, and finds a wreath of rowan on their door. Only Tam Weller half-speaks: 'Your gran made you invisible. Invisible things don't get chosen.' Emotional beat: isolation; the horror of being unwelcome among people who are afraid for you.

chapters.title: Closer Each Day
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The chair in new photographs has moved from the table's end to beside Casper's own seat; a mug appears on it, warm. Casper stops sleeping, starts recording the house itself, and captures a second voice humming Edith's lullaby beneath their own. Emotional beat: paranoia curdling into reluctant belief.

chapters.title: The Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Casper's POV with parish-record excerpts. In the church archive, Casper finds the 1974 baptismal ledger: a page torn out, but the ink ghost remains — a child's name, Hollis Wren, drowned that January, whose grieving parents 'gave him to the house.' Emotional beat: grief revealed as the story's engine; the monster has a history.

chapters.title: They Want You Seated
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The village turns openly hostile after Casper asks about Hollis Wren; someone burns the diary pages left on the porch. In the newest photograph, Casper is sitting in the extra chair, smiling, though they have no memory of it. Emotional beat: terror of losing authorship over one's own image and identity.

chapters.title: Edith's Bargain
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, guided by Tam Weller to the flooded quarry. Tam confesses he helped Edith steal the name in 1974 to save her own daughter — Casper's mother — from being Chosen. The theft unmoored the Guest, and it has spent forty years learning patience. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; every protection was someone else's sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Threshold
chapters.summary: Climax. Casper's POV. On the anniversary night, the house fills with the smell of a long-cold dinner and every mirror shows the table set for two. Casper stands at the threshold and speaks the name — Hollis Wren — returning what Edith took, offering the Guest its seat and its selfhood instead of banishment. Emotional beat: courage as surrender; giving rather than fighting.

chapters.title: A Place at the Table
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, weeks later. The photographs are ordinary again — except one, new, showing two chairs occupied, and Casper feels watched-over rather than hunted. The village sings the song twice now, once for the living and once for Hollis. Casper stays, no longer invisible, no longer alone. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; belonging earned through witness.
